prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: REPEAT

outputs.L1: This is the track I’ve had on REPEAT all afternoon: she is butterfly-brilliant riband, rice-flour face, silken—even her voice a sashed kimono. If I were foolish like her—but aren’t I foolish like her?—spotting the coil of smoke and the billowed sail against the verge of sky, simple on the rise, surveying the anchorage: simple me, signal me, dreading the confident assumption of return; dreading more uncertain tones to come, the thinning notes, the performance too close to my own impatient—swells, a surge: sick wind. But the emotion is, after all, an artfully conjured gesture, an arranged marriage between a past ache and frail woodwinds. I could skip ahead, could break the inconsolable loop of harbor, waiting, overlook, waiting, inevitable waning eye, troubled robins once more in the handkerchief trees; once more, a brief aquarelle of triplet lilies, blue as willowware, in that interval before his embrace falters, stuck, founders. [Shuffle play.] Such a pitch of tenderness in the voice; such an awful lot of noise.
outputs.L2: This is the song I’ve been looping without pause since noon: she gleams like a butterfly, a bright ribbon, her face pale as rice flour, her whole presence smooth as silk; even her singing seems wrapped in a belted kimono. I might call her foolish—yet am I not equally foolish, noticing the spiral of smoke and the sail swelling at the sky’s edge as she crests the hill and looks across the anchorage? Naive me, conspicuous me, afraid of her serene certainty that he will return, and even more afraid of the hesitancy that follows: the notes growing sparse, the performance echoing too closely my own impatient surges and swells. An unhealthy wind blows through it, though the feeling itself is finally only a skillfully manufactured gesture, a marriage arranged between an old sorrow and delicate woodwinds. I could jump forward; I could escape the unbearable cycle: harbor, waiting, overlook, waiting, the unavoidable dimming of the eye. Disturbed robins appear again among trees like handkerchiefs; again, a fleeting watercolor of lilies in triplets, blue as willow-pattern china, during the pause before his embrace weakens, catches, and sinks. [shuffle play] The voice reaches an extraordinary height of tenderness, amid such a dreadful amount of noise.
outputs.L3:
The speaker has been listening to the same song over and over, captivated by a singer who seems at once delicate, elegant, and almost unbearably expressive. Her voice gives shape to images of drifting smoke, distant sails, and a harbor suspended in anxious expectation. Together, these images evoke the dread of waiting for someone whose return is uncertain, as hope slowly gives way to fear.

The feeling seems deeply personal, yet the speaker remains aware that it is also the product of careful artistry: old sorrow has been refined and woven together with the fragile sound of woodwinds. At any moment, the speaker could skip the track and escape its emotional pull. Instead, they remain trapped in its repeating cycle of longing, diminishing hope, and inevitable disappointment. At the center of it all is the singer’s profound tenderness, made even more striking by its contrast with the overwhelming noise that surrounds the performance.
outputs.L4:
I keep playing the song, though “playing” is too mild a word for what I do. I return to it compulsively, restarting it before the final note has fully disappeared, as if repetition might uncover something the first hearing concealed. Each time, I tell myself I am listening more carefully: to the tremor in the singer’s voice, to the faint brush of strings beneath it, to the way a single bright note rises and vanishes like light on water. But attention is only part of it. I am also waiting for the song to change, even though I know exactly what will happen.

Its world is small and intricately made. There is a harbor, or the suggestion of one: ropes darkened by spray, lamps wavering in the wind, boats shifting against their moorings. Someone stands at the edge of the water and watches for a figure who may be returning. The lyrics never say enough to settle the question. Perhaps the beloved has promised to come home. Perhaps that promise was made long ago and has already been broken. Perhaps the person waiting understands this but continues to wait because hope, once given a place to live, does not leave easily.

The imagery is almost too beautiful. Every feeling arrives dressed in ornament—salt caught like silver on a sleeve, clouds compared to torn lace, the moon suspended over the harbor like a pale and watchful eye. Even sorrow is handled delicately. Nothing is allowed to be merely lost; it must drift, gleam, echo, or dissolve. I find myself admiring the precision of these images while also resisting them. Their elegance feels protective, as though the song has placed pain inside a glass case where it can be examined without being touched. Yet the more carefully the pain is arranged, the more sharply I feel it.

The instrumentation works in the same way. It is fragile without being simple. A plucked instrument marks out the first few notes, each one surrounded by silence. Strings enter so quietly that I do not notice them until they are already carrying the melody. Somewhere in the background, a metallic sound rings and fades. It might be a bell, or only a struck string allowed to resonate. The arrangement creates the illusion that everything could break apart at any moment. The singer seems less accompanied than held together.

That fragility is what makes the song difficult to escape. Loud music can push a feeling away by overwhelming it, but this song draws me inward. Its quietness demands participation. I supply the tension it refuses to announce. I lean toward every pause, listening for the next breath, the next footstep on the pier, the next sign that the waiting will end.

It never does.

The narrative circles back on itself. The tide withdraws and returns. The harbor lamps go out and are lit again. The same promise appears in slightly altered language, as if the singer is testing whether different words might make it true. By the final verse, the figure beside the water seems to occupy several moments at once: the first night of waiting, the hundredth night, and the night when waiting has become indistinguishable from a life.

When the song ends, its opening feels inevitable. I begin again.

At first, the repetition comforts me. Nothing inside the song can surprise me. The beloved will remain absent or uncertain; the harbor will remain suspended between departure and arrival; the voice will fracture at the same syllable and recover in the same place. The song’s sadness is contained, measured, and beautifully engineered. Unlike my own anxiety, it obeys a structure. It lasts a fixed number of minutes. It has verses, a refrain, a final chord.

But repetition gradually changes the scale of everything. A phrase that once sounded tender begins to feel insistent. The soft percussion becomes a tapping I cannot ignore. The pauses fill with expectation. Even the singer’s breath seems amplified, until the song’s delicacy becomes its own kind of noise. It does not shout, but it occupies every available space.

By then, I am no longer listening only to the song. I am listening to memories it has disturbed: old departures, unfinished conversations, promises I accepted because disbelief felt more painful. The harbor becomes every place where I have waited for reassurance. The absent figure takes on familiar faces. The singer’s controlled ache merges with my own less graceful fear—the fear that what has gone will not return, and the equal fear that it will return unchanged, bringing the old hurt with it.

Still, I play the song again. I want its tenderness even when that tenderness hurts me. I want the beauty of its images, the careful trembling of its instruments, the world in which pain can be shaped into something luminous. Yet I also want release from it. Each replay offers both possibilities: that the song will soothe me, and that it will finally become unbearable.

Perhaps this is what repetition does to beauty. It brings us close enough to see how it was made, then closer still, until craft and feeling can no longer be separated. The consoling pattern becomes a trap; the fragile sound grows deafening. What seemed at first like a song about waiting by the water becomes the act of waiting itself—circular, ornate, and impossible to conclude.

The last note fades. For a moment, there is silence.

Then I start it over.
outputs.L5:
**REPEAT**

Wake. Work. Rest. Repeat.

At first, repetition feels like a cage: the same alarm, the same roads, the same familiar conversations. Yet repetition is also how we learn. A musician plays the same passage until it becomes effortless. An athlete practices the same movement until instinct takes over. A child repeats a word until it belongs to them.

Not every cycle is pointless. Some routines build strength, trust, and meaning. Others keep us trapped in habits we have outgrown. The challenge is to notice the difference.

Repeat what helps you grow.  
Repeat what brings kindness.  
Repeat what makes you better.

And when the pattern no longer serves you, have the courage to stop—and begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness prose poem about listening to Puccini’s “Un bel dì, vedremo” from *Madama Butterfly* on repeat, blending musical analysis, Japanese imagery, longing, and modern shuffle-play language.
counterfactuals.output:
I put “Un bel dì, vedremo” on repeat, though repeat is not the word—return, perhaps, tide, perhaps the small circular arrow glowing on the screen like a moon that has forgotten how to wane. The orchestra opens a door of pale wood. Beyond it: harbor mist, a paper lantern breathing, a hill where one figure keeps watch until watching becomes a country.

Shuffle is off. Fate is not allowed to improvise.

Her voice rises carefully, almost conversationally, as if hope must first disguise itself as fact: one fine day. The melody climbs by degrees, gathering silk and salt, and Puccini knows the cruelty of restraint—how the strings can hold back the ocean, how a quiet phrase can contain a ship, a marriage, three years of weather. Then the line blooms, not suddenly but inevitably, like ink spreading through handmade paper, like plum blossom opening under late snow because no one has told it the season is wrong.

Track 1 of 1.  
Now playing: longing.  
Up next: longing.

I listen on the train, in a kitchen blue with midnight, under notifications falling soundlessly as cherry petals: your package has shipped, your battery is low, someone has liked the photograph in which I was almost happy. Between alerts, Butterfly waits. In the brass, a distant glint; in the woodwinds, birds skimming Nagasaki water; in the strings, the thin red thread that binds one wrist to another and cuts deeper each time the beloved does not return.

The aria keeps building its impossible house. Here is the path he will take. Here is the hill. Here is the smoke from the ship translated into certainty. Here is the silence she will choose so joy will not be frightened away. The harmony darkens beneath her, but she sings above the knowledge, and that is the wound: the orchestra understands before she does. Or perhaps she understands and sings anyway. Perhaps hope is not ignorance but an instrument, lacquered black, tuned nightly against despair.

Repeat.

The same dawn enters by another window. The same ship appears inside the same measure. My thumb hovers over skip as over a temple bell, but I cannot strike it. I have made a playlist called COME BACK, though no algorithm can distinguish prayer from preference. It recommends more soprano grief, more doomed women in high fidelity. Because you listened to absence, you may also like: absence remastered, absence live, absence with original orchestration.

Outside, rain stipples the glass like a garden of koi seen from below. A neon sign trembles in the puddles. Somewhere a vending machine hums its one-note sutra. I imagine a white crane crossing the harbor, carrying no message. I imagine every torii gate opening onto the same empty sea.

And then the voice reaches that radiant crest again—breath made architecture, promise made pitch—and for a moment I believe in arrival as purely as music believes in resolution. Not because he comes. Not because the world is kind. Because the phrase rises, and rising is its own brief country; because the cadence delays the fall; because one fine day can be replayed until all days borrow its light.

The track ends.

A fraction of digital silence: black water, held breath, the heart buffering.

Then the opening returns, tender and terrible, and I return with it, pressing my ear to the future as if it were a seashell, as if beneath the static I might hear your footsteps coming up the hill, as if repeat were devotion and not refusal, as if the little circular arrow could turn time around.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental first-person music review that begins “this is the track I’ve had on REPEAT all afternoon,” uses no conventional paragraph breaks, and gradually shifts from admiration of the singer to discomfort with the opera’s romanticized tragedy.
counterfactuals.output: this is the track I’ve had on REPEAT all afternoon, letting the soprano’s voice redraw the room each time it rises: first as silver thread, then as flame, then as something almost architectural, a staircase built note by note into air I didn’t know I was holding. I admire the precision of her breath, the soft pressure she places behind each vowel, the way she makes longing sound less like an emotion than a climate. Even the orchestra seems astonished by her. Strings gather at her feet; woodwinds hover like attentive birds. When she reaches the aria’s summit, I feel the familiar surrender—the unreasonable conviction that beauty this exact must also be true. REPEAT. Again she enters, already wounded, already luminous, and I listen more closely to the little fractures in her phrasing, how skillfully she turns pain into ornament. The performance is extraordinary. That is not in doubt. What begins to trouble me is the machinery around it: the libretto tightening like a ribbon at her throat, the plot insisting that her suffering is what makes her singable, that desire becomes profound only when punished. REPEAT, and now the tenor’s declarations feel less like love than elegant possession; the swelling chords seem to usher her toward an ending everyone but she has been promised. I still marvel at the singer—perhaps more fiercely now, because I can hear her intelligence pressing against the walls of the role—but the opera keeps arranging catastrophe as if it were a bouquet. Her fear receives better lighting than her happiness. Her death is granted the music her life was denied. By the final cadence, the tragedy has been polished until it gleams, and I am no longer sure whether I am moved or merely trained to mistake a beautiful cage for transcendence. The applause erupts inside the recording. My hand hovers over REPEAT.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a listener obsessively replaying an aria from *Madama Butterfly*. Describe the voice, orchestration, harbor scene, and doomed hope of return in dense, fragmented, highly poetic prose.
counterfactuals.output:
Again—the needle, the breath, that first pale filament of voice. Butterfly singing not from the throat but from some wound trained into radiance: a soprano held high, silken, almost weightless, then suddenly iron beneath the silk. Around her, the orchestra stirs like weather remembering its violence—hushed strings, woodwinds salt-bright, brass far off as naval smoke; each swelling phrase a tide lifting the impossible.

Nagasaki harbor, blue enamel under noon. The hill. The small house with its paper walls, its vigilant windows. Below: water glazed with distance; roofs, masts, gulls; the white geometry of a ship not yet there. She sees it because she must. A thread of smoke. A flag. A figure climbing the path slowly enough to make waiting holy. She imagines restraint—no running, no cry—only the long vigil behind the screen, night gathering in the garden, stars burning through leaves, the child asleep, dawn at last touching the door.

Replay. Rewind. Again the voice ascends, carrying its frail architecture of certainty over the darkening pit. The listener knows. The orchestra knows. Even the harbor knows, glittering with the cruelty of indifferent water. Return will come malformed: not reunion but sentence, not love but its foreign shadow. Yet she sings the future into being for three minutes more—each note a lantern against fact, each crescendo a white ship entering the blood, each tenderness already edged with the blade that will end it.

Again. The breath. The harbor. The smoke that is not smoke. Hope, magnificent because doomed, opening its wings over the sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a modernist prose poem inspired by Cio-Cio-San waiting for Pinkerton’s ship, with images of smoke, sails, kimonos, willowware, woodwinds, and fading tenderness. Include punctuation disruptions and a “[shuffle play]” aside.
counterfactuals.output:
At Nagasaki the harbor folds itself into willowware: blue bridge, blue water, one impossible figure refusing to move. Cio-Cio-San waits—kimono bright as a wound beneath the white arithmetic of sails. Smoke lifts from the horizon (or is it weather, or news?) and every mast becomes his return.

The woodwinds begin somewhere behind the paper walls: thin birds, polite grief. She arranges tenderness beside the tea, though tenderness has faded at the edges, handled too often, like silk exposed to sun.

[shuffle play]

Now—another ship. No; a cloud. No—his name passing through the mouth of the house. The harbor keeps revising itself: smoke / sails / smoke. Her sleeves remember embraces her body can no longer prove. Morning breaks with a porcelain sound . . . a cup, a promise, the small blue willow bending forever over water—

and still she waits; while the modern world steams in, black-hulled, punctual, without mercy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ornate, self-aware monologue about the guilty pleasure of replaying a beautiful but emotionally manipulative operatic performance, ending with the contrast between “tenderness in the voice” and “an awful lot of noise.”
counterfactuals.output:
Again.

I press the little triangle—the secular icon of resurrection—and once more the curtain lifts upon that exquisitely engineered catastrophe. I know every trapdoor in it. I can hear the violins laying their silver snares; I can feel the soprano’s breath gathering like weather over a doomed city. Even before the first impossible note ascends, haloed in grief, I know precisely what is being done to me.

And yet I consent.

No, more than consent: I collaborate. I dim the lamps. I arrange my face into its most receptive sorrow. I become both victim and stagehand, lowering the chandelier of memory at the appointed moment. Here comes the pause—just long enough to resemble sincerity. Here comes the tremor—placed with the jeweler’s care of a diamond in a crown. Here comes the orchestral swell, that magnificent emotional forgery, signing my name at the bottom of a confession I never intended to make.

How shamelessly beautiful it is.

The heroine suffers with such disciplined abandon that I almost resent real grief for being less musical. Her despair has breath support. Her ruin arrives in perfect pitch. When she forgives the faithless beloved, I forgive people who have never apologized; when she dies, I mourn versions of myself that were never born. It is manipulation, certainly—but manipulation in brocade, manipulation wearing pearls, manipulation descending a staircase while the brass announces the collapse of the human heart.

And I replay it.

I replay it because knowing the mechanism does not dismantle the spell. The painted moon is still a moon if one is lonely enough. The cardboard dagger still flashes. The false tears, magnified by footlights, still find the true wound. Perhaps this is the guilty pleasure: not that I am deceived, but that I cherish the deception; not that the performance overpowers my judgment, but that my judgment buys a ticket, takes its seat, and applauds.

Again, then. Let the strings conspire. Let the diva lift her jeweled anguish into the rafters. Let me call it catharsis when it is indulgence, and art when it is emotional extortion. I will surrender knowingly, luxuriously, absurdly—until the final chord fades and I am left to wonder how much of beauty is tenderness in the voice, and how much is an awful lot of noise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
